title: Throughput tuning field journal
content:
Purpose
-----
Short running journal for the week: capture what we ran in the cluster, surprising observations, microbench numbers, and action items that don't fit into the main sprint doc. This is intentionally conversational — write down failures so others can pick them up quickly.

Summary (high level)
-------------------
- Focus: reduce 95th/99th tail latency during sustained 500rps spikes while keeping throughput cost within target (<= 1.15x baseline token cost).
- Primary knobs exercised: kernel preemption threshold, microbatch sizing heuristics, KV-cache TTL & evict policy, and request-router batch-splitting logic.
- Outcome: saw a 12-18% reduction in 99th latency for chat workloads with long contexts (4k+ tokens) when combining conservative preemption + adaptive microbatch splitting. Cost impact: ~+6% token CPU utilization on average; still within 1.15x.

Day 1 — 2029-05-10 — smoke and baseline recon
------------------------------------------------
Observed: after the weekly deploy (PR 1428), a steady-state test at 480 rps produced intermittent 99th spikes up to 1.9x baseline at ~45m into the run. Spikes correlated with a subset of requests that have initial prompt length > 3.5k tokens and followed by heavy sampling (top-k 40).
Notes:
- Kernel logs (node-a3b) show short-lived scheduler stalls ~200–600ms during batch assembly.
- KV-cache eviction events spiked at the same timestamps; cache lookups for prefetched keys fell from 98% -> 74% for that cohort.
- Router metrics show an increase in average batch size from 6.1 -> 8.9 just before stall, suggesting late arrivals joining batches pushed it over a tipping point causing kernel preemption.

Experiment 1: Lower kernel preemption threshold
- Change: preemption_threshold from 120ms -> 80ms (so long-running batches yield earlier) in the nightly canary.
- Rationale: reduce long-tail stalls caused by heavy batches monopolizing warp resources.
- Result: 99th latency reduced in canary by 9% for same workload; throughput slightly noisier (more small batches).
- Observation: CPU-side context switch overhead increased ~2.1% but latency improvement outweighed it.

Day 2 — 2029-05-11 — KV cache tuning and TTL experiments
----------------------------------------------------------
Hypothesis: high eviction rate during the spike is caused by larger-than-usual KV footprints from long-context prompts; shorten TTL+promote LRU for cohort could help.

Experiment 2A: aggressive LRU promotion for multi-turn chats
- Change: for requests tagged chat:prompts, mark keys with "sticky" tag for 30s window; do not evict sticky keys until window expiry unless memory pressure > 92%.
- Result: cache hit-rate for tagged cohort improved from 74% -> 91% during spike window; 99th latency improved further by ~7% on canary nodes.
- Caveat: memory pressure on those nodes increased by ~4%, pushing us closer to the eviction fallback; need caution for denser multi-tenant pods.

Experiment 2B: TTL shrink for non-chat short-lived keys
- Change: reduce default TTL from 300s -> 90s for one-off prompts and embeddings.
- Result: small decrease in overall memory used; negligible impact on latency but reduced eviction churn in middle-tier nodes.

Day 3 — 2029-05-12 — adaptive microbatch splitting and router heuristics
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Observations: router sometimes forms large batches when a burst of long-context requests coincide with many short ones. Large batch formation increases KV working set and triggers preemption. We tried adaptive split: split batches when variance in input token counts > 2x and long-request fraction > 30%.

Experiment 3: variance-aware batch splitting
- Change: router will split batches where (max_len / median_len) > 2 and avg_batch_size > 6; split into two sub-batches preserving arrival order.
- Result: reduced incidence of "one fat batch" events by 68% in stress runs; overall throughput reduced ~1.8% but 99th tail dropped 12% for long-context tests.
- Note: this interacts poorly with prefetch coalescing. Need to ensure prefetch keys are duplicated to both sub-batches if they share prefixes.

Day 4 — 2029-05-13 — integration run and regressions check
------------------------------------------------------------
Run: integrated preemption threshold = 80ms + sticky LRU for chat cohort + variance-aware splitting across 6 canary nodes for 2 hours at 520 rps with production-like mix.
Metrics:
- 95th latency: -14% vs previous week baseline
- 99th latency: -15% vs previous week baseline
- Token CPU %: +6.2% avg (within target)
- Cache hit (global): improved from 91.3% -> 93.8% during run for critical cohort
- Error rate: unchanged (0.07% -> 0.08%) — small flakiness observed in one node (node-b12) with OOM near end; root cause: sticky keys + GC latency on older pinned instance type.

Post-run triage notes:
- Root cause for node-b12 OOM: machine type c5g-old-8 had < headroom for sticky policy. Action: pin sticky policy only on nodes with mem_headroom > 18GB (see policy draft).
- Prefetch duplication: router currently discards duplicate prefetches when splitting batches; we need a mechanism to mark prefetch as "replicable" if request prefixes overlap. Filed JIRA-RT-3912.

Open questions and risks
------------------------
- Multi-tenant fairness: sticky LRU helps chat cohort but may create starvation for noisy tenants on the same pod. Need to evaluate using admission control or tenant-aware shards.
- Cost model: +6% CPU tokens is acceptable for now, but if traffic grows 2x we hit cost limits. Build an automated simulation that projects cost at +10%, +20% CPU to decide whether to expand autoscale capacity.
- Eviction cascade: tightening TTLs and sticky flags may shift eviction pressure to other nodes. We need a cluster-wide eviction telemetry to detect pressure shifts (dashboard TODO).

Action items (owners)
---------------------
- Jonas: implement prefetch duplication flag and unit tests (PR linked). Target EOD 2029-05-17.
- Rin: add node-label gating for sticky policy (mem_headroom >= 18GB). Rollout plan draft by 2029-05-16.
- Marcus: simulate cost/clamp scenarios for +10% and +20% CPU token utilization; produce projection table for Thursday sync.
- Aisha (me): update Throughput Tuning Playbook with the new preemption baseline and TTL table; add a short FAQ about "sticky" semantics. Also coordinate with SRE to mark affected canaries.

Notes to follow-up in async channels
------------------------------------
- Slack: #runtime-kernel: posted summaries + graphs (sample images attached in slack thread) — see thread ts: 2029-05-13T19:12Z.
- Confluence: short playbook draft updated at https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RT/Throughput+Tuning+Playbook (link in metadata).
- PR: experimental changes submitted in PR 1428 (serving-runtime). Keep PR open until prefetch duplication and node gating are in.

Random micro-observations
-------------------------
- When we lowered preemption threshold to 50ms (in an A/B microtest), latency improved more but pain from context switching killed throughput too much — 80ms is the current sweet spot.
- For long-context synthetic workloads, jitter is lower when we add a soft cap on batch size = 12 for nodes with earlier generation GPUs (older kernels don't hide memory latency as well).

Appendix: quick reproducibility steps
------------------------------------
1) Checkout serving-runtime branch: feature/throughput-field-1428
2) Deploy canary with flags: --preemption-threshold=80 --sticky-chat-ttl=30s --variance-split=true --split-threshold=2.0
3) Run load profile: /bench/profiles/prod-mixed-4k.json at 520 rps for 2h
4) Capture logs: grep "sched-stall" /var/log/serving-runtime/*.log; export KV metrics from /api/admin/kv-metrics?cohort=chat
If anything is unclear ping me (Aisha) or drop a note in #runtime-kernel — I'm on PTO next week but will be in for a 30m sync Wednesday morning.
